2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate concern (item non-response within interviews): No longitudinal follow-up loss applies to this cross-sectional field assessment and all 10 town primary schools were observed, but the authors explicitly report in Section 5 that many students did not respond to interview questions (e.g., water coping strategies are reported for only 13 of 23 interviewed students on PDF Page 6).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable / High concern if interpreted causally: Non-causal qualitative and descriptive field assessment across 7 public and 3 private schools in one town with no statistical or design controls for school- or student-level confounding.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / Adequate for policy framing, weak as an empirical variable: Section 1 accurately identifies Malawi's key national WASH and disability instruments—National Water Policy (2005), National Policy on Equalisation of Opportunities for People with Disabilities (2006), National Sanitation Policy (2008), and Disability Act, Act No. 8 of 2012 (explicitly noting that the 2012 Act does not make institutional inclusive WASH legally binding)—and benchmarks school facilities against WHO (2009) standards, but legal rules are treated as uniform national background context rather than doctrinally dissected or empirically varied across sites.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: School WASH infrastructure was directly observed and physically measured across all 10 schools using a WHO (2009)-adapted checklist, enabling valuable triangulation against self-reports (such as observing students struggle on uneven paths despite reporting no difficulties). However, student interviews suffered from substantial non-response and normalization/reticence, interview guides and translation procedures are unreported, and market adaptation cost figures rely on single-author local price inquiries without engineering or labor validation.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate / Moderate strength: Physical WASH accessibility outcomes were systematically recorded across all 10 schools via an 8-indicator WHO (2009) checklist (Table 1) and direct physical measurements (distances, platform areas, door widths, drophole diameters), complemented by multi-stakeholder qualitative accounts of functional barriers and coping behaviors (such as restricting food and water intake), though incomplete student responses limited experiential outcome completeness.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern / Can't tell: No study protocol or pre-analysis plan is cited, quote selection rules are unreported, and minor numerical inconsistencies appear across the text and tables (e.g., Section 3.4.3 refers to 'Three of ten teachers interviewed' whereas Section 3 and Table 2 report n=11 teachers; Sections 3.1 and 3.2.1 announce 'two' coping strategies or barriers before listing three; Table 3 has truncated digits in its right-most column and total row). Candid reporting of null compliance and study limitations mitigates severe selective-reporting concern.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern: At the school level within Rumphi town, selection bias was minimized by observing all 10 primary schools (7 public, 3 private), though Rumphi town has higher literacy (86%) and prior district inclusive-WASH activity and is not nationally representative. At the student level, purposive sampling sought diversity in age, impairment type, and gender (n=23 across 9 schools), but relied on teacher-supplied lists of students with disabilities (potentially under-identifying less visible impairments given teachers' narrow medical conceptualization of disability) and excluded out-of-school children with disabilities and parents.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: All 10 town primary schools were included; trained special needs teachers (or senior teachers where absent) and district officials were interviewed, and purposive sampling selected up to 4 students per school across 9 schools (1 school had no enrolled children with disabilities) to capture diversity in age (6–18 years), gender, and visual, physical, and cognitive impairments. Limitations include reliance on teacher-compiled lists of disabled pupils and non-inclusion of parents or out-of-school children.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: While observations used an explicit WHO (2009) framework across all 10 schools, interviews were recorded and transcribed, and a degree of thematic saturation is reported, the paper omits the interview guides, interview language/translation procedures, and privacy of school interview settings. Moreover, Section 5 candidly reports that many students did not respond to interview questions, which the authors note may reflect a weakness of the interview methods for eliciting responses from children.

domain_ratings.justification: Although the authors note one instance where direct researcher observation contrasted with a student's normalized self-report, there is no reflexive discussion of the researchers' own positionality, adult/authority-to-child power dynamics (particularly where teachers provided written consent), or potential researcher influence on study formulation, student reticence, and teacher responses.

domain_ratings.justification: Formal ethical approval was obtained from the Republic of Malawi National Commission for Science and Technology (Protocol No. P.11/15/65), transcripts were anonymized, and student assent was obtained alongside written consent from teachers. raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Zaunda et al. (2018) conduct a primary qualitative field assessment of disability-friendly school WASH facilities across all 10 primary schools (7 public, 3 private) in Rumphi town, northern Malawi, triangulating structured WHO (2009)-based facility observations and local adaptation market-cost estimates with interviews of 23 students with disabilities, 11 teachers, and 2 district officials. Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study exhibits Moderate methodological concern (6 Yes, 2 Can't tell [Q5, Q8], 1 No [Q6], plus valuable research contribution on Q10). Key strengths include a complete town-wide school census covering both public and private providers, multi-stakeholder perspectives, and direct physical observations/measurements that revealed normalization of barriers by students and underestimation by teachers. Key methodological weaknesses include omitted interview guides and translation details alongside substantial student non-response during interviews (Q5), absence of researcher reflexivity regarding adult/authority-child power dynamics (Q6), unexplained reliance on teacher rather than parental written consent for day-school minors aged 6–18 (noted under Q7 despite national ethics approval), minimal one-sentence reporting of hand-coding procedures without coder/reliability details (Q8), and exclusion of parents and out-of-school children with disabilities.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (2 Can't tell items [Q5, Q8] and 1 No item [Q6])
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary qualitative field assessment combining qualitative interviews (students with disabilities, teachers, and district officials) with structured WHO-based school facility observations and descriptive local market adaptation cost estimates across 10 primary schools

raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study is explicitly designed, titled, and executed as a primary qualitative field assessment ('A qualitative assessment of disability friendly water and sanitation facilities in primary schools, Rumphi, Malawi'). Although it includes a structured WHO (2009) observation checklist across the 10 town schools (summarized descriptively as counts/percentages in Table 1) and local market price lookups for basic adaptations (Table 3), these serve as descriptive field contextualization and observational triangulation within a small-N qualitative case assessment rather than a separate quantitative survey/statistical study or a formal mixed-methods design, making the CASP Qualitative Checklist the most appropriate appraisal instrument.
